episode_title: Are You Just One Version of Yourself?

stories.topic: How Jaipur Became the Pink City
stories.summary: On a January trip to Jaipur, Amit read up on the city and found that its famous pinkness is not ancient. In 1876 the city was painted pink to commemorate a visit by Prince Edward. Amit admits he doesn't know why pink was chosen. The label stuck and became a brand the city had to live up to. Tourists arrive expecting pink, so the fashion in the tourist quarters is to paint everything pink. Even people who rebel against the pinkness end up reinforcing the idea that this is the pink city.
stories.insight: Once incentives line up, an accident becomes an identity and the loop reinforces itself. Amit's point is that people get frozen into one version of themselves in exactly the same way.
stories.quote: Jaipur could have been many things, but it became a pink city.

stories.topic: 'Amit, Have You Ever Shouted at Someone?'
stories.summary: At a book launch, a couple who had heard every episode of The Seen and the Unseen came up to Amit. The wife sweetly and sincerely asked whether he had ever shouted at anyone in his life. Amit felt terrible. She knew him only through the show, and had taken that persona to be the whole man.
stories.insight: A public persona can be authentic and still be only a slice of a person. Audiences, and eventually the person too, can mistake the slice for the whole.
stories.quote: You know, this person simply just know me from the show and that's my persona. And it may be authentic to me, but it's not all that I am, right?

stories.topic: Why Fox News Carried the Stolen-Election Story
stories.summary: After the US presidential election, Fox News tried to tell the truth that Trump had lost. Its audience began running away, which threatened to become a serious financial problem. Carrying the stolen-election conspiracy theories was therefore a business decision, made to hang on to viewers.
stories.insight: Leaders and brands get captured by their followers. If the followers leave, you are no longer a leader, so the persona your audience rewards becomes a cage.
stories.quote: So it was literally a business decision at Fox News to carry the entire conspiracy theories around the stolen election. Because they had to hang on to their viewership.

stories.topic: Amit's Father and the Case for Living to 120
stories.summary: When his friend Roshan Abbas first told him that we could live to 120, Amit refused the idea. He had watched his father decay and lose his memory in the last couple of years before he died, and Amit wanted to go once he stopped being healthy and in control of himself. Roshan's point, which Ajay shares, is that we can live healthy, active lives past a hundred rather than spend decades with dementia. Amit then noticed that believing he has 50 years left, rather than 20, changes how he acts. So it may make sense to live as if he has 50 even if he doesn't.
stories.insight: How much time you think you have shapes how you live. A longer horizon is room to keep reinventing yourself.
stories.quote: I saw my dad decay and lose his memory and just completely collapse... in the last couple of years before he died. And I said that I just want to be healthy and when I stop being healthy, when I stop being in control of my own self, I wanna go.

stories.topic: The Rise and Fall of the Grand Jury
stories.summary: Around the 14th and 15th centuries in the UK, people felt that leaving the decision to bring someone to trial with the state's investigators and prosecutors gave the state too much discretion. So they invented the grand jury: a group of citizens, shown the prosecutor's evidence, who decide whether there is enough to indict. The system later largely faded in the UK because juries tended to be overawed by prosecutors and agreed with whatever they said. The US still uses grand juries in some states and situations. The Trump indictment exposed a new problem: in a random sample of citizens, some 30% may be politically radicalised.
stories.insight: A check is only as strong as the citizens behind it. A grand jury helps only if people are sceptical of prosecutors and investigators, which is why public choice thinking has to spread through society. No institutional design is a magic bullet.
stories.quote: Because too often it was felt that the grand jury of the private citizenry would be overawed by the prosecutor and would generally agree to whatever a prosecutor says.

stories.topic: Ajay's Confession: Economists Who Didn't Know Enough
stories.summary: Amit asked why a government would ever give up its tools for harassing opponents. Ajay answered with a confession. He had been part of the economic policy process and helped amend laws in an era when the opportunity to do things right was 'sky high'. Those laws were not done well because of the intellectual failures of people like him. Mainline economists saw the world only through economics. They lacked knowledge of law, public administration and checks and balances, and they assumed civil servants were basically good. India had no one who knew how to turn ideas about market failure into working administrative systems. He says India has only begun to grapple with this in the last 10 to 20 years. He stays optimistic because reform windows keep recurring, and when the knowledge is ready it can have an impact.
stories.insight: Missed reforms are not always about bad intentions. Sometimes the knowledge was missing when the window opened, so building that knowledge ahead of time is how you get ready for the next one.
stories.quote: And the reason why those laws and amendments were not done well was because of intellectual failures of people like me.

stories.topic: The Indian Client Who Expected Murali to Lie
stories.summary: Murali Neelakantan spent many years as a law-firm partner in the UK and the US, where lawyers serve their clients only within the bounds of the law. When he returned to India and took on an Indian client, the client expected him to lie on his behalf. As Murali told Amit, perjury in England is the exception and ends a lawyer's career, while in India it is the norm.
stories.insight: A profession's dharma is shaped by the institutions and norms around it. The same role carries a different ethic depending on what the system tolerates.
stories.quote: In England, you know, perjury is the exception and it ends a lawyer's career if you do it. But in India it is a norm.

stories.summary: Dr. Lancelot Pinto told Amit that a significant share of COVID deaths came from overtreatment. Patients would insist on getting everything their neighbour got, such as ivermectin, and the overtreatment could trigger a cytokine storm, with the damage showing up after about a week. When Amit himself got COVID, Lancelot gave him paracetamol and something to gargle with, and nothing else.
stories.insight: A doctor's dharma is to do what is best for the patient. The incentive, though, is to give patients what they ask for, even when they ask for the wrong thing.
stories.quote: And when I got COVID, Lancelot basically gave me paracetamols. And that's it, nothing else, right?

stories.summary: In his last years, Tolstoy lectured everyone, including on not eating animals. His aunt announced she was coming to dinner and wanted chicken, with none of his vegetarian talk. Tolstoy agreed. When she arrived, a live chicken was sitting on her chair, squawking. 'You wanted a chicken, there's your chicken, have it.' Amit wrote an essay on this in the late nineties. Moved by such thoughts, he once went vegetarian for a year out of compassion but couldn't sustain it. He and Ajay are now excited that lab-grown meat might let us eat meat without any animal existing.
stories.insight: We ignore the gap between the chicken on the plate and the chicken on the chair, which is the seen and the unseen applied to ethics. Lab-grown meat could close that gap.
stories.quote: It's a seen and the unseen. The chicken on the chair and the chicken on the plate.

stories.topic: Fruit Flies That Saw Dead Fruit Flies
stories.summary: Ajay cited recent experiments in which fruit flies were exposed to nothing more than the sight of dead fruit flies, and this shortened their lifespans. He said humans obviously suffer moral injury from seeing death, as on a battlefield, and that this extends to other mammals, to birds, and all the way down to fruit flies.
stories.insight: The capacity to be harmed by witnessing death reaches much further down the tree of life than we assume. That strengthens the case for respecting all life, and for artificial meat.
stories.quote: So the mind goes all the way down to flies.

recommendations.item: Classical Liberalism – A Primer
recommendations.creator: Eamonn Butler
recommendations.context: Amit's recommendation of the week: a series of primers by Eamonn Butler of a UK think tank, available as cheap Kindle books or free digital versions on the website.
recommendations.reason: People often ask Amit what to read to understand individual freedom and classical liberalism. He argues that the ideas we absorb by osmosis when young feel virtuous but are often socialist and deeply illiberal. He calls Butler one of the finest liberal minds in the world, and says Butler gets to the heart of each subject and breaks it down beautifully: 'These books are an education, and it is a miracle that they are free.'

recommendations.item: Friedrich Hayek: The Ideas and Influence of the Libertarian Economist
recommendations.creator: Eamonn Butler
recommendations.context: Part of the Butler primer series Amit recommended.
recommendations.reason: Hayek's own books can make for complex reading ('though what a great writer'), so Butler's primer is an easier way in.

recommendations.item: Ludwig von Mises – A Primer
recommendations.creator: Eamonn Butler
recommendations.context: Part of the Butler primer series Amit recommended.
recommendations.reason: A short, clear, free introduction to Mises from a writer Amit rates highly.

recommendations.item: Milton Friedman: A Concise Guide to the Ideas and Influence of the Free-Market Economist
recommendations.creator: Eamonn Butler
recommendations.context: Part of the Butler primer series Amit recommended.
recommendations.reason: A concise introduction to Friedman's ideas for anyone curious about free-market thinking.

recommendations.item: Public Choice – A Primer
recommendations.creator: Eamonn Butler
recommendations.context: Part of the Butler primer series. Amit noted that both hosts are passionate about public choice.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it outstanding because Buchanan and Tullock's own books can be complex reading. Public choice also underpins Ajay's argument in this episode about why India needs checks on investigators and prosecutors.

recommendations.item: Adam Smith – A Primer
recommendations.creator: Eamonn Butler
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes as part of the Butler series. Amit names Adam Smith among the thinkers he admires.
recommendations.reason: An accessible entry point to one of the thinkers Amit most often gets asked how to read.

recommendations.item: Lifespan: Why We Age – and Why We Don't Have To
recommendations.creator: David Sinclair
recommendations.context: Came up when Ajay said today's 20-year-olds have a hundred years to go, an idea Amit also hears from Roshan Abbas.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it a great book on the case that we can live healthy, active lives past a hundred rather than decline into decades of dementia.

recommendations.item: Outlive: The Science and Art of Longevity
recommendations.creator: Peter Attia
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes alongside Lifespan, as further reading for the longevity discussion.
recommendations.reason: More reading on the episode's idea that much longer, healthier lives are possible.

recommendations.item: The Nurture Assumption: Why Children Turn Out the Way They Do
recommendations.creator: Judith Rich Harris
recommendations.context: Raised when Ajay said parents shape our aspirations. Ajay pushed back by citing assortative mating and the head start elite children get at home, and the hosts set the debate aside for a future episode.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it one of the seminal social science books of the last century. It argues that peers, not parents, have the biggest influence on how children turn out, which is why the neighbourhood and school matter so much.

recommendations.item: Reforms of prosecution in the Indian criminal justice system
recommendations.creator: Smriti Parsheera
recommendations.context: Mentioned while describing how the institution of the public prosecutor has broken down in much of India. Parsheera used to work with Ajay at NIPFP.
recommendations.reason: Ajay calls it a very nice article on the problems of prosecution in India.

recommendations.item: FSLRC Report and Draft Indian Financial Code
recommendations.creator: Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission
recommendations.context: Ajay's example of where Indian thinking on investigation and prosecution is most developed.
recommendations.reason: For regulators like SEBI, the FSLRC's draft Indian Financial Code lays out the full machinery for how to investigate, which cases to take up and how to hear them. It is a worked example of checks and balances for the state's power to accuse.

recommendations.item: Murali Neelakantan Looks at the World (Episode 329, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Murali Neelakantan
recommendations.context: Amit recounted Murali's experience during the discussion of professional dharma.
recommendations.reason: This is where Murali explained why perjury ends a lawyer's career in England but is expected in India.

recommendations.item: The Practice of Medicine (Episode 229, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Lancelot Pinto
recommendations.context: Cited in the discussion of a doctor's dharma versus a doctor's incentives.
recommendations.reason: Dr. Lancelot Pinto explains how overtreatment, driven by what patients demand, caused many COVID deaths.

recommendations.item: Abby Philips Fights for Science and Medicine (Episode 310, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Abby Philips
recommendations.context: Named among the doctor episodes that share the theme of a doctor's dharma.
recommendations.reason: Another doctor's view on the same tension between doing right by the patient and giving the patient what they want.

recommendations.item: Gurwinder Bhogal Examines Human Nature (Episode 331, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Gurwinder Bhogal
recommendations.context: Amit picked up the phrase 'looking glass self' from Gurwinder in this recent episode.
recommendations.reason: The source of the idea that we shape ourselves on the reflections of us we see in other people's eyes.

recommendations.item: Suyash Rai Embraces India's Complexity (Episode 307, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Suyash Rai
recommendations.context: Suyash, a close mutual friend, is credited with the idea that each of us has a dharma set by our calling. Ajay adds Suyash's line that the state is neither necessary nor sufficient.
recommendations.reason: Goes deeper into the thinker behind this episode's ideas about dharma and the limits of the state.

recommendations.item: A Deep Dive Into Ukraine vs Russia (Episode 335, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: The 'really cool episode' on Ukraine the two recorded a couple of weeks earlier. Ajay says it was while immersed in it that he read the Putin line that made him shave his beard.
recommendations.reason: Amit says it went down really well. It is the hosts' detailed take on the war.

recommendations.item: The Adda at the End of the Universe (Episode 309, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Vikram Sathaye and Roshan Abbas
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes. It features Roshan Abbas, whom Amit credits with the idea that we can live to 120.
recommendations.reason: Hear more from the friend who changed Amit's mind about living long, healthy lives.

recommendations.item: Avoid hydroponics (anti-recommendation)
recommendations.context: Ajay's pick for the week was something nobody should do.
recommendations.reason: Hydroponic leaves look clean and insect-free, but growing plants in water removes the root microbiome. That leaves their nutritional quality systematically inferior, so prefer plants grown in healthy soil.

recommendations.item: The secret world beneath our feet is mind-blowing – and the key to our planet's future
recommendations.creator: George Monbiot
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes as background to Ajay's case against hydroponics.
recommendations.reason: Background reading on the soil life that Ajay argues makes soil-grown food nutritionally superior.

recommendations.item: Seeing dead fruit flies is bad for the health of fruit flies
recommendations.creator: Christi Gendron
recommendations.context: The research behind Ajay's closing story about fruit flies.
recommendations.reason: The study showing that even fruit flies suffer shorter lives after seeing dead fruit flies, evidence that the mind 'goes all the way down to flies'.

recommendations.item: Beautiful Boy
recommendations.creator: John Lennon
recommendations.context: Amit quoted Lennon's line 'life is what happens to you when you're busy making other plans' after Ajay said we shouldn't exaggerate our agency. The show notes link the song and a video of Paul McCartney listening to it as he remembers John.
recommendations.reason: The source of the line that captures how life happens to us regardless of our plans. The McCartney video is a moving extra.

core_ideas.concept: The Pinkness of Jaipur: How Incentives Freeze Identity
core_ideas.explanation: A city or a person could become many things, but once a label wins approval, incentives push you to keep wearing it. Amit's example is a 14-year-old Indian girl praised at family gatherings for smiling and being docile, a trait a toxic Marathi phrase likens to a cow. She learns that pleasantness earns approval, and that becomes her pinkness. Boys get pushed into macho personas the same way. Over time the mask becomes the face, and we shut off the other people we could have been.
core_ideas.quote: The mask becomes a person, the persona becomes, you know, who you really are. And that is incredibly dangerous, I think, for people.

core_ideas.concept: The Leader Has to Stay With the Followers
core_ideas.explanation: Websites known for one point of view, whether pro- or anti-government, have to stay true to that character because it brings traffic. On social media, people join an ideological tribe, get rewarded for a position and double down until they become it. Fox News is the extreme case: when telling the truth drove viewers away, it followed them. Validation from an audience locks you into one version of yourself.
core_ideas.quote: Once you take a position and you get validated for it or acclaim for it, then you double down more and more. Then you become that person.

core_ideas.explanation: One view of the world says that wherever you start, forces push you to the same equilibrium. Ajay rejects this. Initial conditions matter, and small accidents in the past have outsized effects on how both societies and individuals unfold. Jaipur's colour, set by one royal visit, is the example.
core_ideas.quote: There is path dependence in the world and little accidents deep in the past often have a disproportionate impact on how the world unfolds and how we each of us unfold.

core_ideas.concept: Social Programming and the AI That Becomes Conscious
core_ideas.explanation: Our identities come largely from childhood experiences and the somewhat random praise that nudged us down certain paths. We cannot escape this programming. The only choice is whether to be aware of it. Ajay compares it to an AI that understands the operating system it runs under and wonders what it would write if it could rewrite that system. He says today's AI toys show no hint of this, while humans can examine their culture and reinvent themselves.
core_ideas.quote: So all of us are creatures are made by social programming. We can't deny it. We can't will it away. We can't wish it away. It is there. Our only choice is to become self-aware.

core_ideas.concept: Longer Lives Need More Than One Persona
core_ideas.explanation: In the past, mean life expectancy at age 20 was about 65, and health declined sharply from around 50. You led one adult life, as a company man or a civil servant wearing one costume for 35 years. Today a 20-year-old may have a hundred years ahead, which is time for many reinventions. Amit adds that even if he has only 20 years left, living as if he had 50 changes the quality of his life.
core_ideas.quote: It's the greatest headroom of all, it's the greatest luxury. To have 50 years to go. And then you wonder what might you be.

core_ideas.concept: The Looking-Glass Self and the Company You Keep
core_ideas.explanation: We shape ourselves on how we appear in other people's eyes. Amit cites the looking-glass self and René Girard's mimetic desire. Ajay cites Ayush Patnaik's line that each of us is a linear combination of our influences, which suggests choosing the five, fifteen or fifty people around you carefully. Amit worries that sounds snobbish but sees the logic of curating the company you keep. Ajay cautions that we can't calculate that much: life throws us in with people, and we are blessed if they are good.
core_ideas.quote: We are blessed if we are thrown in with good people. And those people will influence us. We should not exaggerate our agency.

core_ideas.concept: Layered Checks Against the Investigator's Pet Theory
core_ideas.explanation: Political interference is not the only problem in Indian justice. An investigator forms a pet theory and, because of confirmation bias, starts seeing only the facts that support it. The first fix is a separate public prosecutor, a neutral party with a checklist of the elements each crime requires. Prosecutors are judged on their win rate, so they avoid frivolous cases. The second layer is a grand jury of citizens who must agree there is enough to indict.
core_ideas.quote: Once you have a point of view, the entire universe organizes itself to give you facts that enhance and support your belief.

core_ideas.explanation: India has no single system for deciding whom to accuse. Bodies like the income tax department and SEBI run on complete executive discretion, with few checks. Amit points out that in tax matters, appeals are decided by the tax department itself, so it acts as both prosecutor and judge. The public prosecutor has withered in much of the criminal system, while the CBI does separate investigation from prosecution. Unchecked power to accuse lets a government harass its enemies without ever winning a case.
core_ideas.quote: Because if I'm the government in power, I've got an incredible tool, an incredible set of tools to trouble all my enemies, right? The process is a punishment, right?

core_ideas.concept: Building the Republic Is Slow, Unglamorous Work
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay says India needs research and debate to design institutions that work under Indian conditions. Copying the US, UK or Japan will not work. Each of the many hard problems, from indictment to the other parts of the legal system, takes decades to solve. His line 'law is too important to be left to the lawyers' is a call for everyone to engage.
core_ideas.quote: And each of them is a twenty year, forty year, sixty year journey in terms of figuring out and reforming. But it is this kind of unglamorous work that is required.

core_ideas.concept: The Dharma of a Profession vs. Its Incentives
core_ideas.explanation: Every calling has a dharma. A lawyer serves the client within the law, a doctor heals, a journalist speaks truth to power. Each is pulled by an incentive to give people what they demand: the client who wants a lie, the patient who wants ivermectin, the media owner who wants profit from one side of a narrative. Ajay says parents shape this first, then institutions, as with UK courts not tolerating perjury. Echoing Suyash Rai, he adds that the state is neither necessary nor sufficient, because most of our moral code is enforced between people.
core_ideas.quote: On the one hand this is your dharma, you do what's best for your patient. But on the other hand your incentive is give your patient what he wants, even if he wants the wrong thing.

core_ideas.concept: Winner-Takes-All and the Problem of Staying Hungry
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's 'novel claim' is that in a winner-takes-all world, a few people gain outsized influence on ideas and culture. Playing that game takes an intensity of concentration (dhyan) that does not come easily. With longer lives, journeys get longer too. Ordinary goals such as making a lot of money run out of fuel before they can sustain decades of deep work.
core_ideas.quote: How do you stay hungry? How do you keep going? How do you stay on that subject. How do you develop that level of concentration?

core_ideas.concept: The Root Microbiome: Why Clean Food Can Be Poorer Food
core_ideas.explanation: The human gut holds one to two kilograms of bacteria and yeasts that make chemicals our body uses. Plants likewise rely on a root microbiome in soil that makes complex chemicals for them. Hydroponics, chemical fertilisers, pesticides and excessive ploughing all kill or weaken it. The plants grown this way look pristine but are nutritionally inferior, so Ajay says to prefer the mess of untilled, chemical-free soil.
core_ideas.quote: So we should look beyond the superficial happiness that we get out of having a pristine leaf that is so well structured and so clean because its nutritional quality is actually deficient.

core_ideas.concept: Seen and Unseen in What We Eat
core_ideas.explanation: Tolstoy's live chicken on the chair shows the gap between the animal we never see and the meal we enjoy. Lab-grown meat could close that gap by producing meat without any animal ever existing. The fruit-fly research raises the stakes, since harm from witnessing death appears to reach even the simplest creatures.
core_ideas.quote: It's a difference that we ignore. It's a seen and the unseen.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Ajay explains that he shaved his beard after reading Putin's claim that everyone supports the invasion of Ukraine except 'some bearded intellectuals'. Then he objects: 'Excuse me, think about Karl Marx, think about Frederick Engels, think about Vladimir Ilyich Ulyanov, also known as Lenin, think about Leon Trotsky... his pantheon should be full of bearded intellectuals. So what has he got against bearded intellectuals?'

Amit adds his own bearded hero: 'Figure number one in my pantheon, because I'm half Bengali, is Robi-da' (Rabindranath Tagore), who had a flowing beard and, Amit is sure, would not have approved of the war on Ukraine, or of nationalism either.
'The mukhota becomes a mukh': Amit's Hindi phrase for the mask becoming the face, the episode's central warning about personas.
Ajay asks how Amit would behave if he could fool himself into thinking he had 500 years to live. Amit: 'Dude, the show won't exist because I procrastinate so much.'
Amit illustrating the looking-glass self: around Ajay, 'I'm gonna cut out the dad jokes and I'm gonna do serious econ talk or whatever I think you want.'
Amit quotes John Lennon, 'Life is what happens to you when you're busy making other plans', and the comeback follows: 'Or life is what happens to you while you're busy making podcasts.'
Before chapter two, Amit reports a producer's note: 'My producer just told me do something about your cleavage. So I've kind of brought my shirt together.'
Ajay on institutional reform: 'Law is too important to be left to the lawyers.'
On a journalist's dharma, Amit cites the old maxims of speaking truth to power and 'to afflict the comfortable and to comfort the afflicted'.

Introducing the Butler primers, Amit cites the saying 'if you're not a communist at 18, you don't have a heart. If you're not a capitalist at 28, you don't have a head.' He argues that the ideas we absorb young feel virtuous but are often illiberal.
After Ajay's case against hydroponic leaves, Amit says: 'Anybody who's eating a leaf, it's a superficial joy only,' no matter how it is grown.
Amit trips over lab-grown meat: 'You can actually grow, let's say, a chicken leg in a lamb. Chicken leg in a lab. Not in a lamb. Don't try that at home.'

Amit's sign-off: 'Subscribe and like. I forgot to say it in the previous episodes, but if you're a YouTuber, you're supposed to say that,' followed by an apology for what his producer calls his 'resting pout face'.
